summary: Describes the Internet Nomenclator Project, which aims to bring together hundreds of public CCSO servers worldwide. It explains how to register a server and how to use the search engine to find people. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is one search box that looks through many separate phone books around the world at once.

questions: what is the internet nomenclator project
how to search across ccso servers
subtitle: A system for unified searches across many separate CCSO directory servers.

tldr.problem: Hundreds of CCSO servers existed worldwide with different database schemas and attributes, making it difficult to search across multiple servers for a person without knowing which server to query.
tldr.mechanism: The Nomenclator system provides a query resolver that translates queries into a common format, uses a distributed catalog to find relevant servers, caches results, and translates responses back into a unified view.
tldr.outcome: Users can search many CCSO servers at once by querying Nomenclator with a standard schema, avoiding the need to query each server separately or understand their different attribute names.

today: RFC 2258 is an Informational RFC describing the Internet Nomenclator Project and the Nomenclator system architecture. It has not been obsoleted and documents an important research effort to federate distributed directory services.

sections.title: The CCSO Directory Problem
sections.content:
The CCSO (Computing and Communications Services Office) name service protocol became widely deployed at universities and organizations worldwide. However, each CCSO server is independent and has its own database schema (attribute names and data formats). The 300+ CCSO servers use more than 900 different attributes to describe people. Very few attributes are common—only name and email appear in more than 90% of servers.

Without integrated search support, finding a person across multiple servers requires querying each server separately, which is slow and requires understanding each server's attribute names. The Internet Nomenclator Project solves this by providing fast, integrated access to the information in CCSO servers, allowing users to query many servers at once using a unified schema.
sections.eli5: Each office has its own way of storing information about people. Nomenclator learns all their different ways and lets you ask one question that gets answered from all of them.

sections.title: How Nomenclator Works
sections.content:
A Nomenclator system has two main components: a distributed catalog service and a query resolver. The catalog gathers metadata (information about databases) from CCSO servers, including constraints on attribute values, schema mappings, and available data repositories. The query resolver sits at the user's location, accepts queries in a unified schema (the 'world view'), and uses the catalog to find relevant servers.

The resolver translates each global query into local queries for only the relevant servers, avoiding the overhead of contacting all servers. It then translates the responses from each server's local schema back into the world view. The resolver caches both metadata and query results. If a cached answer is recent enough, the resolver returns it immediately without contacting the servers.
sections.eli5: You ask Nomenclator a question in plain language. It asks a librarian which of a thousand offices might have the answer. Only relevant offices are checked. Answers come back and are translated into a consistent format.

sections.title: Query Optimization and Access Functions
sections.content:
Nomenclator uses access functions to find and retrieve data. Catalog functions answer 'where is the data?' by examining constraints and returning a list of relevant servers. Data access functions know how to query a specific server and retrieve results. An active catalog dynamically narrows the search space by examining attribute constraints. For example, if a server only has information about the computer science department at a French university, the catalog marks it as irrelevant for queries about other departments or countries.

Administrators register their servers by providing a schema mapping (how to translate between local and global attributes) and constraints on attribute values (like 'city' or 'state'). A small amount of metadata enables Nomenclator to avoid contacting irrelevant servers, dramatically improving performance while reducing load on the servers.
sections.eli5: Each office tells Nomenclator what kind of people it has (like 'only French computer scientists'). When you ask about all Americans, Nomenclator skips the offices that don't have Americans.

sections.title: Implementation and Future Directions
sections.content:
The Internet Nomenclator Project provides a centralized query service accessible through a web page and the Simple Nomenclator Query Protocol (SNQP, defined in RFC 2259). The system supports exact string matching, wildcard matching, and word-based matching in the style of CCSO services. Query results are timestamped with a 't-bound' (the age of the oldest cached item used), allowing users to request more current data by flushing older cache entries.

The current implementation works with CCSO and relational databases, but the Nomenclator architecture is designed to be extensible to other name services and directory systems. Future phases will provide query cost estimates, advice on constraining queries, and distributed query resolvers at user sites to reduce latency and network load.
sections.eli5: Right now Nomenclator works with CCSO phone books, but it could work with other kinds of directories too. It can learn what information is most recent and let you request fresher answers if you need them.

sections.title: Registration and Usage
sections.content:
CCSO administrators register their servers through the Internet Nomenclator Project home page (cm.bell-labs.com/cs/what/nomenclator). The registration service collects server location and contact information, constraints on entries (like 'city', 'country', 'department'), and a mapping from the local schema to the world view. The mapping is typically only 50 lines long, as most attributes require only one or two lines to map.

Query responses include a t-bound timestamp indicating the freshness of the answer. Users can request more current data by asking for responses newer than the t-bound, which flushes older cache entries. The system maintains a minimum t-bound (some refresh interval earlier than current time), automatically refreshing stale cache entries.
sections.eli5: When an office joins Nomenclator, it tells the system 'here is how we name our attributes' and 'here is what kinds of people we have'. Then Nomenclator can automatically translate questions and answers for that office.

references.text: Elliott, J., and J. Ordille, "The Simple Nomenclator Query Protocol (SNQP)", RFC 2259, January 1998.
